question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 1998, marine biologist Orrin Vessaly proposed that young reef fish steer toward reefs by following the crackling sound made by snapping shrimp.
• Vessaly built his model from playback experiments on coral reefs, where young fish swam toward speakers broadcasting shrimp crackle.
• Snapping shrimp also live in the mangrove-lined estuaries of tropical coasts.
• In 2024, a team led by Mireille Tanvoss played shrimp crackle through speakers in mangrove estuaries.
• Young fish that live in mangrove estuaries swam toward the speakers.
• When the team repeated the playback at coral reefs, young reef fish again swam toward the speakers.

The student wants to present the team's findings as extending, rather than overturning, Vessaly's model. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: In Tanvoss's team's playbacks, young reef fish again swam toward shrimp crackle, as Vessaly's model predicts, and mangrove-estuary fish did so as well, a setting that Vessaly's reef-based playbacks had not covered.
answer_b: Tanvoss's team confirmed Vessaly's model, which he built from coral-reef playbacks, when young reef fish in the team's own reef playbacks again swam toward speakers broadcasting shrimp crackle.
answer_c: Contrary to Vessaly's model, which was built from playback experiments on coral reefs alone, Tanvoss's team found that young fish in mangrove estuaries swam toward shrimp crackle, as young reef fish again did at the reefs.
answer_d: In Tanvoss's playback tests, young fish swam toward speakers broadcasting shrimp crackle both in mangrove estuaries and at coral reefs, the setting of the playback experiments that Vessaly conducted.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer. It accomplishes the goal by presenting the new findings as an extension of Vessaly's model rather than a refutation: it says the reef result held up again, as the model predicts, so the model is not overturned, and it then says the same behavior appears in mangrove estuaries, a setting the reef-based playbacks had not covered, so the model's reach is widened. The details come from the notes, and the stance is carried by the relation between the two settings.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It presents the findings as merely confirming Vessaly's model: it reports only that young reef fish again swam toward shrimp crackle in the setting the model was built on. It leaves out the mangrove-estuary result, so it never shows the model reaching a setting it had not covered, and it does not present the findings as extending the model.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It presents the findings as overturning Vessaly's model by opening with "Contrary to" and stressing that the model came from reefs alone, even though the notes show the reef result was replicated and the mangrove result does not contradict it. That is the opposite of the stated goal.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It reports accurate facts about both settings and notes where Vessaly's experiments took place, but it never says what the results mean for his model. It takes no stance on whether the findings extend or overturn the model, so it does not accomplish the goal.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• The Brakewater Codex is a medieval prayer book whose place of origin is unknown.
• Historian Renata Falkner argues that the codex was made at Ysolt Priory; historian Tobias Wrenfield argues that it was made at Hollin Abbey.
• Dr. Lena Aberash analyzed the codex's ink and found that it has an unusually high copper content.
• Nine of the ten securely dated Ysolt documents that Aberash tested use high-copper ink; two of the ten securely dated Hollin documents do.
• Hollin's account books show that its scribes bought ink from Ysolt in some years.

The student wants to present the ink evidence as favoring Falkner's account over Wrenfield's account without ruling out Wrenfield's account. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: Aberash analyzed the Brakewater Codex's ink, which has an unusually high copper content, and compared it with the ink in ten securely dated documents each from Ysolt Priory and Hollin Abbey, some of which also use high-copper ink.
answer_b: Because the codex's high-copper ink matches nine of ten Ysolt documents but only two of ten Hollin documents, the evidence favors Falkner's account by ruling out Wrenfield's claim that Hollin Abbey made the codex.
answer_c: The codex's high-copper ink matches nine of ten Ysolt documents but only two of ten Hollin documents, which supports Falkner's account; because Hollin's scribes bought Ysolt ink in some years, though, Wrenfield's account remains possible.
answer_d: The codex's high-copper ink matches nine of ten Ysolt documents and two of ten Hollin documents, and because Hollin's scribes bought Ysolt ink in some years, the evidence supports Falkner's account and Wrenfield's account equally.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer. It gives the ink comparison (nine of ten Ysolt documents versus only two of ten Hollin documents) and says this supports Falkner's account, so the evidence leans toward Ysolt. It then notes that Hollin's scribes bought Ysolt ink in some years, which means high-copper ink in the codex could have reached Hollin and Wrenfield's account remains possible. This is exactly the relation the student wants: the evidence tilts toward Falkner's account without eliminating Wrenfield's.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It reports accurate details about the analysis, but it takes no stance on either account. It never mentions Falkner or Wrenfield, never says which monastery the ink matches better, and never says what the evidence means for the competing explanations, so it does not present the evidence as favoring Falkner's account.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It presents the evidence as favoring Falkner's account, but it overstates what the notes support by claiming the evidence rules out Wrenfield's claim. Two of the ten Hollin documents use high-copper ink, and Hollin's scribes sometimes bought ink from Ysolt, so Hollin Abbey remains possible. The goal explicitly calls for not ruling out Wrenfield's account.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It mentions both the ink matches and the purchases of Ysolt ink, but it concludes that the evidence supports the two accounts equally. Nine of ten matches versus two of ten means the evidence is not balanced; the goal is to present it as favoring Falkner's account over Wrenfield's.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2011, plant physiologist Daria Selwick reported that brushing seedlings of a small mustard-family plant twice daily made their stems shorter than those of unbrushed seedlings.
• Her study compared 24 brushed seedlings with 24 unbrushed seedlings.
• Brushed stems in Selwick's study were 31% shorter on average than unbrushed stems.
• In 2023, a team led by Pavan Ostergaard repeated the experiment using Selwick's brushing protocol.
• The 2023 study compared 180 brushed seedlings with 180 unbrushed seedlings.
• Brushed stems in the 2023 study were 8% shorter on average than unbrushed stems, a difference that was statistically distinguishable from zero.

The student wants to present the 2023 results as confirming the direction, but not the size, of the effect Selwick reported. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: Selwick's 31% shortening of brushed seedling stems did not hold in the 2023 repeat, in which the Ostergaard team, using 180 seedlings per group, found an 8% difference between brushed and unbrushed stems.
answer_b: The Ostergaard team confirmed Selwick's 2011 finding that brushing shortens seedling stems, repeating her protocol with 180 seedlings per group and finding the difference statistically distinguishable from zero.
answer_c: Using Selwick's brushing protocol, the Ostergaard team compared 180 brushed and 180 unbrushed seedlings in 2023 and found brushed stems 8% shorter on average, a difference statistically distinguishable from zero.
answer_d: Selwick's finding that brushing shortens seedling stems held up in the 2023 repeat, but the Ostergaard team, testing 180 seedlings per group, found brushed stems only 8% shorter, against the 31% she had reported.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer. It presents the 2023 results as confirming that brushing shortens seedling stems ("held up") while showing that the effect was much weaker than originally reported: stems were only 8% shorter, against Selwick's 31%. That is exactly what the goal asks for, since the repeat study agrees with the original study about which way brushing affects stems but does not agree about how large the effect is.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It reports the same figures accurately, but it frames the 2023 results as a failure of Selwick's finding ("did not hold") and describes only "a difference" without saying that brushed stems were shorter. It therefore does not present the 2023 results as confirming the direction of Selwick's effect.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It presents the 2023 results as confirming Selwick's finding that brushing shortens stems, but it never mentions that the 2023 effect (8%) was far smaller than the 31% she reported. The goal requires that the size of the original effect not be confirmed, and this choice leaves that discrepancy out, so it reads as a full confirmation.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It accurately reports the 2023 procedure and the 8% result, but it takes no stance toward Selwick's earlier finding: it never mentions her 31% result or says whether the 2023 outcome agrees with hers. It is a neutral report of the new data, not a presentation of those data as confirming one aspect of her effect and not another.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• A museum's bass viol was long attributed to the instrument maker Ingolf Brevik and catalogued as made in 1725.
• Brevik worked in the town of Sandvarre from 1688 until his death in 1731.
• In 2023, conservator Anneli Dunmere analyzed the tree-ring pattern in the viol's spruce top.
• The pattern matched a reference chronology in which the wood's last ring formed in 1696.
• Based on the usual interval between felling and use, she estimated that the viol was made between 1698 and 1705.
• The viol's neck joint and internal bracing match those of instruments signed by Brevik.

The student wants to present the discovery as revising when, rather than by whom, the viol was made. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: Because Brevik worked in Sandvarre from 1688 until 1731 and the viol's neck joint and internal bracing match those of his signed instruments, both the 1725 catalog date and the attribution to Ingolf Brevik remain in place.
answer_b: Conservator Anneli Dunmere analyzed the tree-ring pattern in the viol's spruce top, which matched a reference chronology with a last ring formed in 1696, and estimated that the viol was made between 1698 and 1705.
answer_c: Anneli Dunmere's tree-ring analysis, which dates the viol's spruce top to a chronology ending in 1696 rather than to 1725, calls into question the long-held attribution of the viol to Ingolf Brevik, who worked in Sandvarre until 1731.
answer_d: Although Anneli Dunmere's tree-ring analysis indicates that the viol was made between 1698 and 1705 rather than in 1725, the viol's neck joint and internal bracing and Ingolf Brevik's working years of 1688 to 1731 leave Brevik as the viol's likely maker.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer. It presents the discovery as changing the date while leaving the maker intact. It states the new date (between 1698 and 1705 rather than 1725), then notes that the viol's neck joint and internal bracing match Brevik's signed instruments and that the new date falls within Brevik's working years (1688 to 1731), so Brevik remains the likely maker. The date is revised and the maker is not, which is the stance the student wants.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. The facts it cites are accurate, but its conclusion ignores the tree-ring analysis: it presents the discovery as changing nothing, keeping both the 1725 catalog date and the attribution to Brevik. The student wants to show that the date was revised, and this choice never mentions the tree-ring analysis or the new date of between 1698 and 1705.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It reports the tree-ring analysis and the new estimated date accurately, but it takes no stance on the maker. It never mentions the old 1725 date, so nothing is shown as revised, and it never says whether Brevik remains the maker, so it does not present the discovery as revising when but not by whom the viol was made. It is a neutral report of the finding, not the framing the student wants.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It uses accurate details from the notes, but it frames the tree-ring result as casting doubt on the attribution to Brevik. The notes show that the new date falls within Brevik's working years and that the viol's construction matches his signed instruments, so the discovery revises the date, not the maker. The student wants to present it as revising when, rather than by whom, the viol was made, and this choice reverses that.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 1994, Maren Nordell reported that the kittiwake colony on Vaskel Island had declined steeply, by about 40 percent, over the previous twelve years.
• Nordell counted the colony's nests by viewing the cliffs from a boat offshore.
• In 2021, Ilse Bexley found that nests on upper ledges are hidden from the water, so boat counts omit them.
• Bexley counted nests in aerial photographs taken of the island during the same twelve years.
• The photographs show every ledge, including the upper ledges.
• Bexley's counts show a decline of about 36 percent over the twelve years.

The student wants to present Bexley's reanalysis as a challenge to the method, but not to the conclusion, of Nordell's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: Bexley's aerial-photograph counts, which show every ledge, discredit Nordell's study, whose boat counts omitted upper-ledge nests and reported a decline of about 40 percent in the colony.
answer_b: Bexley's aerial-photograph counts show that Nordell's boat counts omitted upper-ledge nests, yet the same photographs still show a colony decline of about 36 percent, near the 40 percent Nordell reported.
answer_c: Bexley's aerial-photograph counts, which show every ledge, agree with Nordell's boat counts: a decline of about 36 percent in the photographs matches the roughly 40 percent decline Nordell reported.
answer_d: Nordell counted nests from a boat offshore and reported a decline of about 40 percent, while Bexley counted nests in aerial photographs from the same twelve years and found a decline of about 36 percent.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer. The goal asks for a framing in which Bexley's reanalysis challenges how Nordell counted the nests but leaves Nordell's conclusion standing. Choice B does exactly this. It says the boat counts omitted upper-ledge nests, which is the challenge to the method. It then says the photographs still show a decline of about 36 percent, near the 40 percent Nordell reported, which shows that the conclusion survives the reanalysis. Every detail comes from the notes.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. This choice reports accurate facts but frames the reanalysis as discrediting Nordell's whole study. The notes show that Bexley's counts still found a decline of about 36 percent, so they do not undermine Nordell's conclusion. The choice challenges both the method and the conclusion, when the goal is to challenge the method only. It also never mentions Bexley's own decline figure.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. This choice reports accurate figures, but it presents Bexley's counts only as agreeing with Nordell's. It never mentions that the boat counts omitted upper-ledge nests, so it presents no challenge to the method. The goal requires a challenge to the method, and this choice supplies only the support for the conclusion.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. This choice accurately reports both researchers' methods and both decline figures, but it takes no stance. It does not say that the boat counts omitted nests or that the new figure supports the original conclusion, so it relates Bexley's work to Nordell's in neither way. It simply lists facts, so it does not present the reanalysis as a challenge to the method but not to the conclusion.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Geologists have long explained chains of volcanic seamounts with the hotspot hypothesis: a plate drifts over a fixed plume of hot rock, so seamounts are older the farther they lie from the chain's active end.
• This age pattern has been confirmed in many seamount chains around the world.
• Dr. Mira Danvell's team dated rock samples from nine seamounts in the Kestrane Chain.
• Eight of the nine have ages that rise steadily with distance from the active end, as the hotspot hypothesis predicts.
• The ninth, Ilmarsh Seamount, is about 14 million years older than its position in the chain predicts.
• The team notes that Ilmarsh's age matches neither the hotspot hypothesis nor the main rival, the fracture hypothesis.

The student wants to present the Ilmarsh result as a puzzle for, rather than evidence against, the hotspot hypothesis. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: Eight of the nine dated seamounts follow the age pattern the hotspot hypothesis predicts, while Ilmarsh, about 14 million years older than its position predicts, fits neither that hypothesis nor the fracture hypothesis and so remains unexplained.
answer_b: Because eight of the nine dated seamounts follow the age pattern the hotspot hypothesis predicts, the hypothesis holds for the Kestrane Chain, and the single exception, Ilmarsh, about 14 million years older than its position predicts, is outweighed by the other eight.
answer_c: Ilmarsh Seamount, about 14 million years older than its position predicts, counts as evidence against the hotspot hypothesis, even though eight of the nine dated seamounts follow its age pattern and Ilmarsh fits the fracture hypothesis no better.
answer_d: Dr. Danvell's team dated nine seamounts in the Kestrane Chain and found that eight have ages rising with distance from the active end, while the ninth, Ilmarsh, is about 14 million years older than its position predicts.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer. It reports that eight of the nine seamounts follow the pattern the hotspot hypothesis predicts, and it says that Ilmarsh, which is about 14 million years older than its position predicts, fits neither the hotspot hypothesis nor the fracture hypothesis, so its age remains unexplained. Because the anomaly matches no rival explanation either, it is presented as an open question that the hotspot hypothesis has not yet accounted for, rather than as evidence that the hypothesis is wrong.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It reports the dating results accurately but adds a conclusion the notes don't state, and it uses the eight matching seamounts to present the hotspot hypothesis as settled and treats Ilmarsh as outweighed, a minor exception that needs no explanation. It does not present Ilmarsh as an unexplained result that the hypothesis has yet to account for, so it does not frame the result as a puzzle.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It reports the findings accurately but stops at description. It never relates Ilmarsh to the hotspot hypothesis or states that Ilmarsh remains unexplained, so it does not frame the result as a puzzle that the hypothesis has yet to account for.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It reports the dating results accurately, but it presents Ilmarsh as counting as evidence against the hotspot hypothesis, which is the framing the student wants to avoid. The notes say only that Ilmarsh does not fit; they do not say the hypothesis has been undermined, especially since eight of the nine seamounts fit it and the rival hypothesis fits Ilmarsh no better.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Archaeologists have long debated whether people in the Tessavel highlands were cultivating chickpeas by 10,000 years ago.
• In 2024, archaeologist Daniela Quist analyzed charred chickpeas excavated from Vorrask Cave.
• The chickpeas were radiocarbon dated to about 10,500 years ago.
• Their seeds are about 30% larger on average than seeds of wild chickpeas that grow in the nearby hills.
• Seed size alone cannot establish cultivation: wild chickpeas growing in nutrient-rich soil, such as soil around long-used camp sites, can also produce larger seeds.
• Quist notes that people camped in Vorrask Cave for thousands of years.

The student wants to present the Vorrask Cave find as strengthening, but not settling, the case that people were cultivating chickpeas by 10,000 years ago. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: Because wild chickpeas growing in nutrient-rich camp-site soil can also produce larger seeds, the Vorrask seeds, though about 30% larger than wild chickpeas, have no bearing on whether people were cultivating chickpeas by 10,000 years ago.
answer_b: The Vorrask seeds, dated to about 10,500 years ago and 30% larger than wild chickpeas, support early cultivation, yet wild chickpeas in nutrient-rich camp-site soil might also grow larger.
answer_c: The Vorrask seeds, which are about 30% larger than wild chickpeas, rule out nutrient-rich camp-site soil as the explanation, leaving cultivation by 10,500 years ago as the only account.
answer_d: Archaeologists have long debated whether people in the Tessavel highlands were cultivating chickpeas by 10,000 years ago, and the Vorrask seeds, dated to about 10,500 years ago, are 30% larger than wild chickpeas.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer. It presents the find as support for early cultivation (the seeds date to about 10,500 years ago and are 30% larger than wild chickpeas) while noting that the case is not closed, because wild chickpeas growing in nutrient-rich camp-site soil might also produce larger seeds. That combination makes the find strengthen the claim without settling it.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. Its facts are accurate, but it dismisses the find entirely, saying the seeds have no bearing on the question. The notes show that seeds 30% larger than wild ones, dated to about 10,500 years ago, are consistent with cultivation even though they cannot prove it, so the find does add support to the case. This choice treats the possibility of rich soil as cancelling that support rather than as the reason the case is not settled.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It reports the seed measurements accurately, but it claims the size difference rules out the alternative explanation of nutrient-rich soil and leaves cultivation as the only account. The notes say rich soil can also produce larger seeds, so the alternative remains possible and the case is not settled in the way this choice implies.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It accurately reports the debate and the size and date of the seeds, but it never relates the find to the claim. It takes no stance on whether the find strengthens the case, and it does not say why the case is not settled.
